question: Why does Twitter use a hybrid approach combining write fan-out and read-side merging for user timelines?
reference_answer: For most users, tweets are fanned out into followers' home timeline caches at write time. For celebrities with a very large number of followers, fan-out would mean an enormous number of writes, so their tweets are fetched separately and merged into the timeline when it is read.
notes: orig id 2. Original gold page 11 (PDF 33) only introduces the two approaches; the hybrid is on printed 13 (PDF 35).

question: 2PC vs 3PC
reference_answer: Two-phase commit (2PC) guarantees atomic commit but is a blocking protocol: it can get stuck waiting for the coordinator to recover. Three-phase commit (3PC) is a proposed nonblocking alternative, but it assumes a network with bounded delay and nodes with bounded response times, which most real systems cannot guarantee.

question: A storage engine keeps its data files sorted by key. How does that let it find a key without holding every key in memory?
reference_answer: It can use a sparse in-memory index: one key for every few kilobytes of segment file is sufficient, because a few kilobytes can be scanned very quickly.
evidence_terms: one key for every few kilobytes
notes: From agent batch 2, orig id 9. Question rewritten: the original contained the phrase sparse in-memory index (keyword leakage). Reference answer reworded to the book; the original said one key per block of disk.

question: Why does a B-tree write each piece of data to disk more than once?
reference_answer: A B-tree index must write every piece of data at least twice: once to the write-ahead log and once to the tree page itself. There is also overhead from writing an entire page at a time even if only a few bytes changed.
notes: From agent batch 2, orig id 10. Question rewritten: the original asked for the cause of write amplification in B-trees, but the book uses that term for log-structured indexes on this page. The 4 KB figure in the original answer is not in the text.

question: A client holds a lock, pauses for a long time, then writes to storage after its lock has expired. How can the storage service protect itself from that stale write?
reference_answer: Every time the lock server grants a lock or lease it also returns a fencing token, a number that increases every time a lock is granted. The storage service rejects a write carrying a token older than one it has already processed.
notes: From agent batch 2, orig id 11. Question rewritten: the original contained the term fencing tokens.

question: What is the key timing property that distinguishes linearizability from eventual consistency?
reference_answer: Linearizability is a recency guarantee: the value read is the most recent, up-to-date value, not one from a stale cache or replica.
notes: From agent batch 2, orig id 12.

question: What is the difference between checking data structure when reading versus checking structure when writing in document stores?
reference_answer: Schema-on-read means the structure of the data is implicit and only interpreted when the data is read. Schema-on-write is the traditional relational approach where the schema is explicit and the database ensures all written data conforms to it.
notes: From agent batch 2, orig id 13. Good paraphrase: the question avoids both terms.

question: Why do log-structured storage engines use probabilistic set membership structures for key lookups?
reference_answer: Looking up a key that does not exist is slow because the memtable and every segment back to the oldest must be checked. A Bloom filter is a memory-efficient structure for approximating the contents of a set; it can tell you a key does not appear and saves unnecessary disk reads.
notes: From agent batch 2, orig id 14. Good paraphrase: the question avoids the term Bloom filter.

question: How can an application be built by composing specialized storage and processing systems around dataflow, instead of relying on one monolithic database?
reference_answer: By unbundling databases: composing specialized storage and processing systems with application code, an approach also known as the database inside-out approach.

question: What happens when a leaderless database accepts writes on reachable nodes outside a key's designated home nodes during a network outage?
reference_answer: It uses a sloppy quorum: writes are accepted on reachable nodes that are not among the designated home nodes, and once the interruption is fixed, hinted handoff sends those writes to the home nodes.
notes: From agent batch 2, orig id 16. Both terms also co-occur on PDF 201, 206, 356 and in the index; check the chunk boundaries.

question: What are the trade-offs between LSM-trees and B-trees regarding write throughput versus read throughput?
reference_answer: LSM-trees are typically faster for writes, whereas B-trees are thought to be faster for reads. Reads are slower on LSM-trees because they have to check several data structures and SSTables at different stages of compaction.
evidence_terms: LSM-trees are typically faster for writes
notes: From agent batch 2, orig id 17. Original answer said B-trees are typically faster for reads; the book says thought to be.

question: How do document-partitioned (local) secondary indexes compare to term-partitioned (global) secondary indexes?
reference_answer: With document-partitioned indexes each partition maintains its own secondary index, so a read must query all partitions (scatter/gather). Term-partitioned indexes cover all data, so a read can go to one partition, but writes are slower and more complicated.
notes: From agent batch 2, orig id 18. Original gold page was the range 17-19 (invalid) and the term scatter-gather is not verbatim. Names both concepts in the question, so it favours keyword search.

question: How does a broadcast hash join differ from a reduce-side sort-merge join in MapReduce?
reference_answer: A broadcast hash join loads the small input entirely into a hash table in each mapper and scans the large input, with no sorting or reducer. A sort-merge join sorts and partitions both inputs by join key so matching keys reach the same reducer.
notes: From agent batch 2, orig id 19. Evidence is nine pages apart, so a chunker with small chunks must retrieve both places. Names both concepts in the question.

question: What is the operational difference between a stream-stream join and a stream-table join?
reference_answer: A stream-stream (window) join matches events from two streams within a time window. A stream-table join enriches a stream of events by looking up records in a table kept up to date.
notes: From agent batch 2, orig id 20. Original had no gold page. Names both concepts in the question.
